claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-ISH data and cited reference.

claims.claim: 20.4% of all S1pr3+ cells expressed Npy2r.
claims.source: S1pr3+ cells also co-expressed Npy2r (20.4% of all S1pr3+), a marker of a subset of mechanonociceptive A fibers (Arcourt et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-ISH data and cited reference.

claims.claim: S1pr3 was expressed in 70.6% of Scn1a+ cells.
claims.source: S1pr3 was expressed in 70.6% of Scn1a+ cells and 72% of Npy2r+ cells, comprising a majority of both of these populations.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-ISH data.

claims.claim: S1pr3 was expressed in 72% of Npy2r+ cells.
claims.source: S1pr3 was expressed in 70.6% of Scn1a+ cells and 72% of Npy2r+ cells, comprising a majority of both of these populations.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-ISH data.

claims.claim: 67.1% of all S1pr3+ cells were Trpv1+ and/or Trpa1+ C nociceptors.
claims.source: The remaining S1pr3+ cells were Trpv1+ and/or Trpa1+ C nociceptors (67.1% of all S1pr3+), which are reported to overlap minimally with the Scn1a+ and Npy2r+ populations (Arcourt et al., 2017; Osteen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-ISH data and cited references.

claims.claim: 42.4% of S1PR3+ cells co-stained with anti-Peripherin.
claims.source: We found that 42.4% of S1PR3+ cells co-stained with anti-Peripherin, demonstrating that S1PR3 is expressed in a subset of small-diameter neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data from S1pr3mCherry/+ reporter mice.

claims.claim: 69.5% of S1PR3+ cells co-stained with anti-NF200.
claims.source: We also observed that 69.5% of S1PR3+ cells co-stained with anti-NF200, which marks medium and large-diameter myelinated neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data from S1pr3mCherry/+ reporter mice.

claims.claim: S1PR3+ cells were primarily of small to medium diameter (11.3–35.1 µm).
claims.source: Furthermore, we observed that S1PR3+ cells were primarily of small to medium diameter (11.3–35.1 µm), whereas all cells in the DRG ranged from 11.3 to 53.9 µm.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell diameter measurements from IHC data.

claims.claim: Only 56.1 ± 22.4% of mCherry-expressing neurons were activated by 1 µM S1P.
claims.source: Interestingly, only 56.1 ± 22.4% of mCherry-expressing neurons were activated by 1 µM S1P (Representative trace in Figure 4B; representative images in Figure 4C), which our dose-response showed to be the saturating concentration for calcium influx (Figure 4D; EC50 = 155 nM).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claims.claim: All S1P-responsive neurons were also capsaicin-sensitive (n > 2000 neurons).
claims.source: All S1P-responsive neurons were also capsaicin-sensitive (n > 2000 neurons).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data from over 2000 neurons.

claims.claim: The mean diameter of S1P-responsive mCherry+ neurons was 22.4 ± 1.0 µm.
claims.source: The mean diameter of S1P-responsive mCherry+ neurons was 22.4 ± 1.0 µm, whereas the mean diameter of non-responsive mCherry+ neurons was 28.7 ± 3.2 µm (p=0.0002, two-tailed t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell diameter measurements from calcium imaging experiments.

claims.claim: The mean diameter of non-responsive mCherry+ neurons was 28.7 ± 3.2 µm.
claims.source: The mean diameter of S1P-responsive mCherry+ neurons was 22.4 ± 1.0 µm, whereas the mean diameter of non-responsive mCherry+ neurons was 28.7 ± 3.2 µm (p=0.0002, two-tailed t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell diameter measurements from calcium imaging experiments.

claims.claim: S1P evoked action potential firing in capsaicin-sensitive small diameter cells.
claims.source: We also performed whole cell current clamp experiments and, consistent with other studies (Mair et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2006; Li et al., 2015), found that S1P evoked action potential firing in capsaicin-sensitive small diameter cells (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4E and cited references.

claims.claim: 44.2 ± 15.1% of Hm1a-responsive neurons expressed mCherry.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that 44.2 ± 15.1% of Hm1a-responsive neurons expressed mCherry (Figure 4F), consistent with our staining showing expression of S1pr3 in AM nociceptors and the role of Hm1a-responsive neurons in mediating mechanical pain in vivo (Osteen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4F and cited reference.

claims.claim: S1P dramatically lowered the threshold to fire action potentials (rheobase) in an S1PR3-dependent manner.
claims.source: However, S1P dramatically lowered the threshold to fire action potentials (rheobase) in an S1PR3-dependent manner (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: S1P triggered a robust increase in input resistance.
claims.source: By contrast, S1P triggered a robust increase in input resistance (Figure 5B), consistent with the closure of potassium channels.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The current inhibited by S1P application was carried by potassium.
claims.source: I-V analysis revealed that the current inhibited by S1P application was carried by potassium (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by I-V analysis data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: S1P significantly reduced slow, voltage-dependent tail current amplitudes in an S1PR3-dependent manner.
claims.source: Additionally, S1P significantly reduced slow, voltage-dependent tail current amplitudes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F; Figure 5D (top)) in an S1PR3-dependent manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, center).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: The KCNQ2/3-selective inhibitor XE 991 completely occluded the effects of S1P on tail current.
claims.source: To address whether KCNQ2/3 channels mediated S1P-dependent neuronal excitability, we applied the KCNQ2/3-selective inhibitor XE 991 and found that it completely occluded the effects of S1P on tail current (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Linopirdine occluded the effects of S1P on tail current.
claims.source: Similar results were observed with the related antagonist, linopirdine (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The effect of S1P on KCNQ2/3 currents exhibited an IC50 of 48 nM with saturation at 100 nM.
claims.source: We also found that the effect of S1P on KCNQ2/3 currents was mediated by low levels of S1P, exhibiting an IC50 of 48 nM with saturation at 100 nM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: S1PR3 KO AM nociceptors displayed reduced sensitivity in their force-response relation (slope for HET versus KO: 50 Hz/N versus 35 Hz/N).
claims.source: Compared to S1PR3 HET, S1PR3 KO AM nociceptors displayed reduced sensitivity in their force-response relation (slope for HET versus KO: 50 Hz/N versus 35 Hz/N), as well as attenuated firing over the noxious, but not innocuous, range of mechanical stimulation (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The median von Frey threshold to elicit firing in AM nociceptors was significantly higher in S1PR3 KO animals (3.92 mN) compared to littermate controls (1.56 mN).
claims.source: Strikingly, the median von Frey threshold to elicit firing in AM nociceptors was significantly higher in S1PR3 KO animals (3.92 mN) compared to littermate controls (1.56 mN; Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: S1PR3 KO AM nociceptors displayed a right-shifted cumulative response curve to force-controlled stimuli (50% effective force for HET versus KO: 33.7 versus 60.0 mN).
claims.source: Furthermore, S1PR3 KO AM nociceptors displayed a right-shifted cumulative response curve to force-controlled stimuli (50% effective force for HET versus KO: 33.7 versus 60.0 mN; Figure 6C), consistent with the mechanonociceptive hyposensitivity observed in vivo.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Neither AM conduction velocities nor the conduction velocity distributions of Aβ, Aδ, and C fibers differed between genotypes.
claims.source: By contrast, neither AM conduction velocities nor the conduction velocity distributions of Aβ, Aδ, and C fibers differed between genotypes (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by conduction velocity measurements shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: S1PR3 KO animals displayed a significantly lower proportion of Adapting AM nociceptors compared with littermate controls.
claims.source: S1PR3 KO animals displayed a significantly lower proportion of Adapting AM nociceptors compared with littermate controls (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: S1PR3 KO mice failed to develop thermal hypersensitivity relative to heterozygous littermates at both 24 and 48 hr post-CFA injection.
claims.source: Strikingly, S1PR3 KO mice failed to develop thermal hypersensitivity (Figure 7A; see Figure 7—source data 1) relative to heterozygous littermates at both 24 and 48 hr post-CFA injection.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CFA inflammatory pain model data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: S1PR3 KO animals developed robust mechanical hypersensitivity when thresholds were normalized to account for baseline differences.
claims.source: In stark contrast, S1PR3 KO animals developed robust mechanical hypersensitivity when thresholds were normalized to account for the dramatic baseline differences between knockouts and control animals (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CFA inflammatory pain model data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Flow cytometry experiments showed robust infiltration of immune cells into hindpaw skin from both S1PR3 KO and littermate controls.
claims.source: Consistent with the development of mechanical hypersensitivity, flow cytometry experiments showed robust infiltration of immune cells into hindpaw skin from both S1PR3 KO and littermate controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: Acute blockade of S1P production with SKI II reversed CFA heat hypersensitivity.
claims.source: Acute blockade of S1P production with SKI II or S1PR3 with TY also reversed CFA heat hypersensitivity (Figure 7C), demonstrating that peripheral S1P actively signals via S1PR3 to promote CFA-evoked heat hypersensitivity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological blockade data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Acute blockade of S1PR3 with TY reversed CFA heat hypersensitivity.
claims.source: Acute blockade of S1P production with SKI II or S1PR3 with TY also reversed CFA heat hypersensitivity (Figure 7C), demonstrating that peripheral S1P actively signals via S1PR3 to promote CFA-evoked heat hypersensitivity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological blockade data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Acute S1P/S1PR3 blockade with SKI II or TY elevated mechanical thresholds to pre-CFA, baseline levels.
claims.source: Furthermore, acute S1P/S1PR3 blockade with SKI II or TY elevated mechanical thresholds to pre-CFA, baseline levels (Figure 7D) showing that S1PR3 tunes mechanical pain under normal and inflammatory conditions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological blockade data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: S1P signaling via S1PR3 is a key pathway that tunes mechanical pain sensitivity.
claims.source: We now show that S1P signaling via S1PR3 is a key pathway that tunes mechanical pain sensitivity.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: S1P/S1PR3 sets baseline mechanical pain thresholds.
claims.source: First, S1P/S1PR3 sets baseline mechanical pain thresholds.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by behavioral and electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Depletion of baseline, endogenous S1P induces mechanical hyposensitivity.
claims.source: Depletion of baseline, endogenous S1P induces mechanical hyposensitivity and nanomolar levels of exogenous S1P are sufficient to restore normal mechanical pain sensitivity after depletion.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SKI II injection experiments shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Nanomolar levels of exogenous S1P are sufficient to restore normal mechanical pain sensitivity after depletion.
claims.source: Depletion of baseline, endogenous S1P induces mechanical hyposensitivity and nanomolar levels of exogenous S1P are sufficient to restore normal mechanical pain sensitivity after depletion.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by S1P rescue experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Elevated micromolar S1P levels promote thermal, but not mechanical hypersensitivity.
claims.source: Second, elevated micromolar S1P levels, such as those produced during inflammation or disease, promote thermal, but not mechanical hypersensitivity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by S1P injection experiments shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The effects of S1P on acute mechanical pain and thermal hypersensitivity are completely lost in S1PR3 knockout animals.
claims.source: The effects of S1P on acute mechanical pain and thermal hypersensitivity are completely lost in S1PR3 knockout animals, which are otherwise normal with respect to other somatosensory behaviors.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from S1PR3 KO mice shown in Figures 1 and 7.

claims.claim: S1PR3 is indispensable for normal function of AM nociceptors, including the adapting AM population.
claims.source: Our study demonstrates that S1PR3 is indispensable for normal function of AM nociceptors, including the adapting AM population, recently discussed in Arcourt et al., that innervates the epidermis and encodes noxious touch (Arcourt et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6 and cited reference.

claims.claim: S1PR3 signaling modulates KCNQ2/3 channels to regulate excitability of A mechanonociceptors.
claims.source: We show that S1PR3 signaling modulates KCNQ2/3 channels to regulate excitability of these A mechanonociceptors (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5 and summarized in Figure 8.

claims.claim: KCNQ channels mediate excitability of Aδ fibers.
claims.source: Other studies have shown that KCNQ channels mediate excitability of Aδ fibers (Schütze et al., 2016; Passmore et al., 2012) and are required for normal mechanonociceptive responses in dorsal horn neurons receiving Aδ input (Passmore et al., 2012), and that opening KCNQ2/3 channels directly with retigabine alleviates pain in vivo (Xu et al., 2010; Hayashi et al., 2014; Blackburn-Munro and Jensen, 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Opening KCNQ2/3 channels directly with retigabine alleviates pain in vivo.
claims.source: Other studies have shown that KCNQ channels mediate excitability of Aδ fibers (Schütze et al., 2016; Passmore et al., 2012) and are required for normal mechanonociceptive responses in dorsal horn neurons receiving Aδ input (Passmore et al., 2012), and that opening KCNQ2/3 channels directly with retigabine alleviates pain in vivo (Xu et al., 2010; Hayashi et al., 2014; Blackburn-Munro and Jensen, 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: S1pr3 and Kcnq2/3 are highly expressed in human sensory ganglia.
claims.source: Finally, S1pr3 and Kcnq2/3 are highly expressed in human sensory ganglia (Ray et al., 2018; Flegel et al., 2015) and recordings from human stem cell-derived sensory neurons show that KCNQ2/3 channels play a key role in mediating their excitability (Young et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Recordings from human stem cell-derived sensory neurons show that KCNQ2/3 channels play a key role in mediating their excitability.
claims.source: Finally, S1pr3 and Kcnq2/3 are highly expressed in human sensory ganglia (Ray et al., 2018; Flegel et al., 2015) and recordings from human stem cell-derived sensory neurons show that KCNQ2/3 channels play a key role in mediating their excitability (Young et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: Thermal hypersensitivity in the CFA model is dependent on TRPV1 ion channels.
claims.source: For example, thermal hypersensitivity in the CFA model is dependent on TRPV1 ion channels (Caterina et al., 2000) and independent of immune cell infiltration (Ghasemlou et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Thermal hypersensitivity in the CFA model is independent of immune cell infiltration.
claims.source: For example, thermal hypersensitivity in the CFA model is dependent on TRPV1 ion channels (Caterina et al., 2000) and independent of immune cell infiltration (Ghasemlou et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: Infiltration of a subset of myeloid immune cells is required for mechanical hypersensitivity in an inflammatory pain model.
claims.source: By contrast, infiltration of a subset of myeloid immune cells is required for mechanical hypersensitivity in an inflammatory pain model (Ghasemlou et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: S1P is a key component of the inflammatory soup that triggers thermal hypersensitivity in the CFA model.
claims.source: Here we show that S1P via S1PR3 signaling is a key component of the inflammatory soup that triggers thermal hypersensitivity in the CFA model.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CFA model data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: S1P signaling via S1PR1 allows for the continuous circulation of lymphocytes between blood, lymph, and peripheral tissues.
claims.source: Outside of the nervous system, S1P signaling via S1PR1 allows for the continuous circulation of lymphocytes between blood, lymph, and peripheral tissues (Matloubian et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: Fingolimod is prescribed as an immunosuppressant for multiple sclerosis treatment.
claims.source: Indeed, fingolimod, a non-selective S1PR modulator, is prescribed as an immunosuppressant for multiple sclerosis treatment (Brinkmann et al., 2010), but the possibility that some of its therapeutic effects may also be mediated via the nervous system has not been fully explored.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference and established medical knowledge.

claims.claim: Intrathecal fingolimod reduces bone cancer pain.
claims.source: Likewise, one study found that intrathecal fingolimod reduces bone cancer pain (Grenald et al., 2017), and while analgesia was attributed to effects on S1PR1 in glia, some of the benefits may be due to S1PR3 signaling in DRG neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: Thermal pain is detected by thermosensitive TRP channels in subsets of nociceptors.
claims.source: Thermal pain is detected by thermosensitive TRP channels in subsets of nociceptors (Caterina et al., 2000; Vriens et al., 2011), and gentle touch is detected by Piezo2 channels in low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs) (Ranade et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Gentle touch is detected by Piezo2 channels in low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs).
claims.source: Thermal pain is detected by thermosensitive TRP channels in subsets of nociceptors (Caterina et al., 2000; Vriens et al., 2011), and gentle touch is detected by Piezo2 channels in low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs) (Ranade et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Aδ high-threshold mechanoreceptors (HTMRs) play a key role in responses to painful mechanical stimuli.
claims.source: Aδ high-threshold mechanoreceptors (HTMRs) have been shown to play a key role in responses to painful mechanical stimuli (Arcourt et al., 2017; Ghitani et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: The Npy2r+ subpopulation of HTMRs mediates fast paw withdrawal responses to pinprick stimulation and terminates as free nerve endings in the epidermis.
claims.source: The Npy2r+ subpopulation of HTMRs mediates fast paw withdrawal responses to pinprick stimulation and terminates as free nerve endings in the epidermis (Arcourt et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: The Calca+ subpopulation of circumferential-HTMRs responds to noxious force and hair pulling, and terminates as circumferential endings wrapped around guard hair follicles.
claims.source: The Calca+ subpopulation of circumferential-HTMRs responds to noxious force and hair pulling, and terminates as circumferential endings wrapped around guard hair follicles (Ghitani et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: Somatostatin-expressing interneurons of laminae I-III in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord receive input from nociceptors and are required for behavioral responses to painful mechanical stimuli.
claims.source: Additionally, somatostatin-expressing interneurons of laminae I-III in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord receive input from nociceptors and are required for behavioral responses to painful mechanical stimuli (Duan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: S1P is a bioactive lipid that signals via 5 G-protein coupled S1P Receptors (S1PRs 1–5).
claims.source: S1P is a bioactive lipid that signals via 5 G-protein coupled S1P Receptors (S1PRs 1–5).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of S1P signaling.

claims.claim: S1P signaling, mainly via S1PR1, plays a well-known role in immune cell migration and maturation.
claims.source: S1P signaling, mainly via S1PR1, plays a well-known role in immune cell migration and maturation (Spiegel and Milstien, 2003; Matloubian et al., 2004; Schwab et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: S1PRs are expressed throughout the nervous system.
claims.source: Additionally, recent studies have shown that S1PRs are expressed throughout the nervous system (Janes et al., 2014; Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013) and S1P signaling is associated with a variety of neuroinflammatory disorders, including multiple sclerosis (Brinkmann et al., 2010) and Alzheimer's disease (Couttas et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: S1P signaling is associated with multiple sclerosis.
claims.source: Additionally, recent studies have shown that S1PRs are expressed throughout the nervous system (Janes et al., 2014; Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013) and S1P signaling is associated with a variety of neuroinflammatory disorders, including multiple sclerosis (Brinkmann et al., 2010) and Alzheimer's disease (Couttas et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: S1P signaling is associated with Alzheimer's disease.
claims.source: Additionally, recent studies have shown that S1PRs are expressed throughout the nervous system (Janes et al., 2014; Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013) and S1P signaling is associated with a variety of neuroinflammatory disorders, including multiple sclerosis (Brinkmann et al., 2010) and Alzheimer's disease (Couttas et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: S1P has been implicated in spontaneous pain.
claims.source: S1P has been implicated in spontaneous pain (Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013) and thermal pain hypersensitivity (Mair et al., 2011; Finley et al., 2013; Weth et al., 2015), but due to conflicting accounts of S1P receptor expression in the CNS (Janes et al., 2014; Weth-Malsch et al., 2016) and PNS (Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Usoskin et al., 2015) as well as inconsistent reports on the effects of S1P on neuronal excitability (Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2006; Li et al., 2015) and pain behaviors (Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Finley et al., 2013; Weth et al., 2015), the role of S1P in somatosensation remains controversial.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: S1P has been implicated in thermal pain hypersensitivity.
claims.source: S1P has been implicated in spontaneous pain (Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013) and thermal pain hypersensitivity (Mair et al., 2011; Finley et al., 2013; Weth et al., 2015), but due to conflicting accounts of S1P receptor expression in the CNS (Janes et al., 2014; Weth-Malsch et al., 2016) and PNS (Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Usoskin et al., 2015) as well as inconsistent reports on the effects of S1P on neuronal excitability (Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2006; Li et al., 2015) and pain behaviors (Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Finley et al., 2013; Weth et al., 2015), the role of S1P in somatosensation remains controversial.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Transcriptome analysis of the sensory ganglia innervating the tactile organ of the star-nosed mole revealed enrichment of several components of the S1P pathway, including S1pr3.
claims.source: To identify candidate genes underlying mechanosensation, we previously performed transcriptome analysis of the sensory ganglia innervating the ultra-sensitive tactile organ (the star) of the star-nosed mole (Gerhold et al., 2013). Immunostaining revealed the tactile organ is preferentially innervated by myelinated Aδ fibers (Gerhold et al., 2013), which are primarily mechanosensitive. While our original analysis focused on ion channels enriched in the neurons of the star organ, our dataset also revealed enrichment of several components of the S1P pathway, including S1pr3.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis data and cited reference.

claims.claim: Single-cell RNA seq of mouse dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons revealed S1pr3 expression in a subset of myelinated mechanoreceptors and a subpopulation of peptidergic C nociceptors.
claims.source: Likewise, single-cell RNA seq of mouse dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons revealed S1pr3 expression in a subset of myelinated mechanoreceptors (Usoskin et al., 2015) in addition to a subpopulation of peptidergic C nociceptors.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA seq data and cited reference.

claims.claim: S1P promotes excitability in small-diameter, capsaicin-sensitive nociceptors.
claims.source: S1P promotes excitability in small-diameter, capsaicin-sensitive nociceptors (Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2006; Li et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: S1PR3 has been shown to mediate spontaneous pain triggered by elevated S1P and thermal sensitization following sterile tissue injury.
claims.source: In addition, S1PR3 has been shown to mediate spontaneous pain triggered by elevated S1P and thermal sensitization following sterile tissue injury (Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: S1P application did not change membrane potential in medium-diameter S1pr3mCherry/+ dissociated DRG neurons.
claims.source: In these cells, 1 µM S1P application did not change membrane potential (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; see Figure 5—source data 1) or elicit firing in the absence of current injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: S1P did not elicit firing in the absence of current injection in medium-diameter S1pr3mCherry/+ dissociated DRG neurons.
claims.source: In these cells, 1 µM S1P application did not change membrane potential (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; see Figure 5—source data 1) or elicit firing in the absence of current injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5A.

claims.claim: S1P had no effect on voltage-gated sodium currents in S1PR3+ medium-diameter cells.
claims.source: We found that S1P had no such effects on S1PR3+ medium-diameter cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E.

claims.claim: S1P had no effect on steady-state potassium currents in S1PR3+ medium-diameter cells.
claims.source: We found that S1P had no such effects on S1PR3+ medium-diameter cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E.

claims.claim: Tail currents in Aδ neurons are primarily mediated by KCNQ2/3 potassium channels.
claims.source: As tail currents in Aδ neurons are primarily mediated by KCNQ2/3 potassium channels (Schütze et al., 2016; Passmore et al., 2012), we postulated that S1P may alter tail currents through modulation of these channels.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Under normal conditions, AM nociceptors set mechanical pain thresholds.
claims.source: Under normal conditions, AM nociceptors set mechanical pain thresholds (Osteen et al., 2016; Abrahamsen et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Under inflammatory conditions, the combined activity of both non-sensitized AM fibers and sensitized C fibers determines overall post-inflammatory mechanical thresholds.
claims.source: By contrast, under inflammatory conditions, the combined activity of both non-sensitized AM fibers and sensitized C fibers determines overall post-inflammatory mechanical thresholds (Lennertz et al., 2012; Abrahamsen et al., 2008).

results.result: S1PR3 KO mice and pharmacological blockade of S1PR3 with TY 52156 selectively impair mechanical pain responses without affecting innocuous touch, thermal pain, itch, or other somatosensory behaviors. S1PR1 blockade has no effect on baseline mechanical or thermal thresholds.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 provide converging evidence from genetic knockout (C1-C6) and pharmacological blockade (C7-C10) approaches showing selective deficits in noxious mechanical sensitivity. The specificity is demonstrated by normal responses in multiple control behaviors (tape removal, righting reflex, heat, itch). Statistical significance is reported with appropriate controls.

results.result: Endogenous S1P is required for normal mechanical pain sensitivity. Depletion of S1P with SKI II reduces mechanical sensitivity, while nanomolar concentrations of exogenous S1P rescue this hyposensitivity. However, micromolar S1P does not induce mechanical hypersensitivity but does trigger thermal hypersensitivity and spontaneous pain.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C15 demonstrate a dose-dependent relationship between S1P levels and mechanical pain. The rescue experiment (C15) with dose-response data provides strong evidence for constitutive S1P signaling. The differential effects of S1P concentrations on mechanical versus thermal pain (C13-C14) are well-documented with appropriate controls.

results.result: S1PR3 is expressed in approximately 43% of DRG neurons, including mechanonociceptive Aδ fibers (Scn1a+, Npy2r+) and C nociceptors (Trpv1+, Trpa1+). S1PR3+ cells are primarily small to medium diameter (11.3-35.1 μm) and include both myelinated (NF200+) and unmyelinated (Peripherin+) neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C24 provide comprehensive characterization of S1PR3 expression using multiple complementary approaches (ISH, IHC, reporter mice). Quantitative data with specific percentages and cell diameter measurements are provided. The expression pattern is consistent across different methodologies.

results.result: Only 56% of S1PR3+ neurons respond to S1P with calcium influx (EC50=155 nM), and all S1P-responsive neurons are capsaicin-sensitive with smaller diameters (22.4 μm) compared to non-responsive S1PR3+ neurons (28.7 μm). S1P evokes action potential firing in capsaicin-sensitive cells, and 44% of Hm1a-responsive mechanonociceptors express S1PR3.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C30 demonstrate functional heterogeneity within S1PR3+ neurons using calcium imaging and electrophysiology. The EC50 determination (C25), statistical comparison of cell diameters (C27-C28), and correlation with Hm1a responsiveness (C30) provide strong evidence. Sample sizes are adequate (n>2000 for C26).

results.result: S1P lowers action potential threshold (rheobase) in S1PR3+ medium-diameter neurons without changing resting membrane potential. S1P inhibits KCNQ2/3 potassium channels, as evidenced by increased input resistance, reduced tail currents, and complete occlusion by KCNQ2/3 inhibitors XE 991 and linopirdine. The effect has an IC50 of 48 nM.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C37 establish the molecular mechanism through systematic electrophysiology experiments. The occlusion experiments with selective KCNQ2/3 inhibitors (C35-C36) provide strong evidence for the target. The IC50 determination (C37) is consistent with behavioral rescue data. Controls with S1PR3 KO neurons demonstrate specificity.

results.result: S1PR3 KO AM nociceptors display reduced mechanosensitivity with decreased force-response slopes (35 vs 50 Hz/N), elevated von Frey thresholds (3.92 vs 1.56 mN), and right-shifted force-response curves. Conduction velocities are normal, but the proportion of Adapting AM nociceptors is significantly reduced in KO animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 provide direct evidence for altered AM fiber function using ex vivo skin-nerve recordings. Multiple complementary measures (force-response, von Frey threshold, cumulative response) converge on reduced mechanosensitivity. The normal conduction velocities (C41) rule out developmental defects. Appropriate littermate controls were used.

results.result: In the CFA inflammatory pain model, S1PR3 KO mice fail to develop thermal hypersensitivity but develop normal mechanical hypersensitivity when normalized for baseline differences. Immune cell infiltration is normal in KO mice. Acute pharmacological blockade of S1P production or S1PR3 reverses CFA-induced thermal hypersensitivity and returns mechanical thresholds to baseline levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 demonstrate distinct roles for S1PR3 in inflammatory thermal versus mechanical hypersensitivity. The normalization approach (C44) appropriately accounts for baseline differences. Flow cytometry data (C45) rules out immune defects. Pharmacological reversal experiments (C46-C48) demonstrate active signaling rather than developmental compensation.

results.result: In medium-diameter S1PR3+ neurons, S1P does not change resting membrane potential, elicit spontaneous firing, or affect voltage-gated sodium or steady-state potassium currents.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 establish what S1P does NOT do in mechanonociceptors, distinguishing these effects from those in small-diameter nociceptors. This negative data is important for understanding the selective mechanism and is supported by electrophysiology recordings with appropriate controls.

results.result: S1PR3-mCherry reporter mice show 48.3% of cultured DRG neurons express the fusion protein, consistent with ISH data. S1PR3 KO neurons do not respond to S1P but show normal capsaicin responses. No differences in neuronal subtype markers or cell diameters are observed between WT and KO DRG.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C111 validate the reporter mouse model and demonstrate that S1PR3 deletion does not cause developmental loss of neuronal subtypes. The consistency between reporter expression and ISH (C104) and normal capsaicin responses in KO neurons (C107) are important controls. Statistical comparisons of cell populations and diameters support the conclusion.

results.result: S1PR3 is not expressed in specialized mechanoreceptors (hair follicle receptors, Merkel afferents) but is expressed in free nerve endings. Skin innervation patterns are normal in S1PR3 KO mice, indicating no developmental loss of sensory innervation.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C115 define the anatomical specificity of S1PR3 expression and rule out developmental innervation defects. The IHC data with multiple neuronal markers and statistical analysis of fiber density (C114) provide adequate evidence. This supports the interpretation that behavioral phenotypes reflect functional rather than developmental deficits.

results.result: S1PR3 KO AM fibers show attenuated firing in the noxious but not innocuous range, with increased non-responders and decreased Adapting AMs. The remaining mechanosensitive fibers show normal firing frequencies, suggesting the deficit is specific to the Adapting AM population.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C120 provide detailed characterization of AM fiber subtypes affected by S1PR3 deletion. The analysis distinguishes between Adapting and Non-adapting AMs (C118) and identifies the specific population affected. The inference in C119 is reasonable given the supporting data, though it remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: S1PR3 mediates baseline mechanical sensitivity but is not required for CFA-evoked mechanical hypersensitivity. However, S1PR3 is required for CFA-evoked thermal hypersensitivity, and acute blockade demonstrates that S1PR3 actively tunes mechanical pain under both normal and inflammatory conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C125 synthesize the CFA model results and distinguish between developmental requirements and acute signaling. The pharmacological blockade experiments (C124-C125) are critical for demonstrating active signaling. The interpretation is well-supported by the data, though the mechanism underlying the differential effects on mechanical versus thermal hypersensitivity could be explored further.

results.result: S1P/S1PR3 signaling constitutively sets baseline mechanical pain thresholds through modulation of KCNQ2/3 channels in AM nociceptors. Baseline nanomolar S1P is necessary and sufficient for normal mechanical pain, while elevated micromolar S1P selectively promotes thermal but not mechanical hypersensitivity. The effects are completely S1PR3-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C137 represent summary and interpretive statements that integrate the major findings. These conclusions are well-supported by the collective experimental evidence from behavioral, electrophysiological, and pharmacological studies. The model of constitutive versus elevated S1P signaling is consistent with all presented data.

results.result: S1PR3 is indispensable for normal AM nociceptor function and modulates KCNQ2/3 channels to regulate excitability. KCNQ channels mediate Aδ fiber excitability and are required for mechanonociceptive responses. S1pr3 and Kcnq2/3 are highly expressed in human sensory ganglia, and KCNQ2/3 channels regulate excitability in human stem cell-derived sensory neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60, C89, C138-C139 integrate current findings with prior literature on KCNQ channels. The citations to prior work (C57-C60, C89, C138-C139) are appropriate and support the mechanistic interpretation. The connection to human relevance (C59-C60) is based on cited literature rather than new data but is appropriately presented.

results.result: Thermal and mechanical hypersensitivity in inflammatory pain models have distinct mechanisms. Thermal hypersensitivity depends on TRPV1 and is independent of immune infiltration, while mechanical hypersensitivity requires myeloid cell infiltration. S1P/S1PR3 signaling is a key component of the inflammatory soup triggering thermal hypersensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C67 contextualize the findings within the broader literature on inflammatory pain mechanisms. The cited references (C61-C63, C65-C67) support the statements about distinct mechanisms. The integration with current findings (C64) is appropriate, though the claim about S1P being a "key component" could be considered somewhat strong given that other mediators also contribute.

results.result: Background on somatosensory mechanisms and S1P signaling: Different sensory modalities are mediated by distinct molecular mechanisms and cell types. S1P signals through 5 GPCRs and plays roles in immune function and neuroinflammatory disorders. Prior studies implicated S1P in pain, but the role remained controversial due to conflicting reports. Transcriptome analysis of star-nosed mole and mouse DRG revealed S1pr3 enrichment in mechanosensory neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C84 provide background context from established literature and the authors' prior work. The citations are appropriate and accurately represent prior knowledge. The identification of S1pr3 enrichment in star-nosed mole (C81) and mouse DRG (C82) provides the rationale for the current study. These are primarily literature review claims rather than new results.

results.result: Under normal conditions, AM nociceptors set mechanical pain thresholds, while under inflammatory conditions, both AM and C fibers contribute. All cells express sphingosine kinases required for S1P production, but conditional knockout approaches cannot completely eliminate S1P. RNA-seq suggests somatosensory neurons have the machinery to produce S1P, but the cellular source remains to be determined.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C95 provide mechanistic context from literature (C90-C94) and acknowledge limitations in identifying S1P sources (C95). The citations are appropriate. The acknowledgment that the cellular source of S1P is unknown (C95) is an important caveat, though it does not undermine the main findings about S1PR3 function.

results.result: Prior studies show that mechanosensory function involves complex molecular specialization. Piezo2-hypomorphic mice have normal pain behavior despite reduced AM fiber responsiveness, and different Piezo2 splice variants have different force sensitivities. S1PR3 and KCNQ channels are enriched in star-nosed mole tactile neurons and co-expressed in mouse myelinated mechanoreceptors. S1P has been linked to inflammatory disorders, and S1PR3 may contribute to neurogenic inflammation in conditions like asthma.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C103 provide additional context from literature relating to mechanosensation complexity, molecular specialization, and clinical relevance. The citations are appropriate and support the discussion points. The connection to star-nosed mole (C99) and potential clinical applications (C101-C103) are reasonable extensions of the findings.
